claims.claim: DS-inhibited neurons as a population were more inhibited on trials with a response.
claims.source: DS-inhibited neurons (67 units) were also more inhibited on trials with a response (Figure 3F and I; t[66]=–4.66, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) and reference to Figures 3F and I.

claims.claim: CS+ excited neurons as a population were more excited on trials with a response.
claims.source: Similarly, CS+ excited neurons (174 units) were more excited on trials with a response (Figure 4G and J; t[174]=10.08, p<0.001), though CS+ inhibited neurons (82 units) did not distinguish between trials with and without a response (Figure 4H and J; t[81]=.479, p=0.633; Bayes factor: null is 6.46 times more likely than the alternative).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) and reference to Figures 4G and J.

claims.claim: CS+ inhibited neurons as a population did not distinguish between trials with and without a response.
claims.source: Similarly, CS+ excited neurons (174 units) were more excited on trials with a response (Figure 4G and J; t[174]=10.08, p<0.001), though CS+ inhibited neurons (82 units) did not distinguish between trials with and without a response (Figure 4H and J; t[81]=.479, p=0.633; Bayes factor: null is 6.46 times more likely than the alternative).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test and Bayes factor) and reference to Figures 4H and J.

claims.claim: Post-DS firing was significantly more predictive of port entry likelihood than post-CS+ firing.
claims.source: Post-DS firing was significantly more predictive of port entry likelihood than post-CS+ firing (Figure 4C and D; t[704]=3.49, p<0.001), though post-cue firing was predictive of port entry likelihood for both the instrumental task (t[313]=3.708, p<0.001), and the Pavlovian task (t[391]=2.697, p=0.0073).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison (t-test) and reference to Figures 4C and D.

claims.claim: Post-cue firing was predictive of port entry likelihood for both the instrumental and Pavlovian tasks.
claims.source: Post-DS firing was significantly more predictive of port entry likelihood than post-CS+ firing (Figure 4C and D; t[704]=3.49, p<0.001), though post-cue firing was predictive of port entry likelihood for both the instrumental task (t[313]=3.708, p<0.001), and the Pavlovian task (t[391]=2.697, p=0.0073).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-tests) for both tasks.

claims.claim: The post-DS firing rate of 62 units (19.75%) significantly predicted the animal's latency to make a port entry.
claims.source: The post-DS firing rate of 62 units (19.75%) significantly predicted the animal's latency to make a port entry (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis and reference to Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Only 14 units (3.57%) had post-CS+ firing rates that significantly predicted port entry latency.
claims.source: By contrast, only 14 units (3.57%) had post-CS+ firing rates that significantly predicted port entry latency (Figure 5C), a much lower proportion of the population (DS versus CS+ % correlated: x2 = 47.477, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis and reference to Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The proportion of latency-predicting neurons is significantly lower in the Pavlovian task than in the instrumental task.
claims.source: By contrast, only 14 units (3.57%) had post-CS+ firing rates that significantly predicted port entry latency (Figure 5C), a much lower proportion of the population (DS versus CS+ % correlated: x2 = 47.477, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison (chi-squared test) of proportions.

claims.claim: The proportion of units with true post-DS firing that predicted the real latency was well outside the distribution of significantly correlated units from the shuffled datasets.
claims.source: The proportion of units with true post-DS firing that predicted the real latency was well outside the distribution of significantly correlated units from the shuffled datasets (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), whereas the proportion of units in the Pavlovian task was not (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with shuffled control data and reference to supplementary figures.

claims.claim: The proportion of units in the Pavlovian task that predicted latency was not outside the distribution from shuffled datasets.
claims.source: The proportion of units with true post-DS firing that predicted the real latency was well outside the distribution of significantly correlated units from the shuffled datasets (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), whereas the proportion of units in the Pavlovian task was not (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with shuffled control data and reference to supplementary figures.

claims.claim: Only 9 units (2.8%) predicted latency in the Pavlovian task when assessed against shuffled latencies.
claims.source: In addition, when we assessed the number of units with post-cue firing rates that were more predictive of the real latency than of the shuffled latencies (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D), we found only 9 units (2.8%) that predicted latency in the Pavlovian task, versus 61 in the instrumental task (19.42%).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with shuffled control data and reference to supplementary figures.

claims.claim: 61 units (19.42%) predicted latency in the instrumental task when assessed against shuffled latencies.
claims.source: In addition, when we assessed the number of units with post-cue firing rates that were more predictive of the real latency than of the shuffled latencies (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D), we found only 9 units (2.8%) that predicted latency in the Pavlovian task, versus 61 in the instrumental task (19.42%).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with shuffled control data and reference to supplementary figures.

claims.claim: Latency-predicting neurons are, on average, significantly excited by presentations of the DS.
claims.source: Furthermore, while latency-predicting neurons are, on average, significantly excited by presentations of the DS (Figure 5D and G; t[61]=7.08, p<0.001; 48/62 units excited, 77.4%), latency-predicting neurons in the CS+ task are not (Figure 5E and H; t[13]=2.00, p=0.06650; 7/14 units excited; Bayes factor of 1.27 in favor of the alternative).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) and reference to Figures 5D and G.

claims.claim: Latency-predicting neurons in the CS+ task are not significantly excited by the CS+.
claims.source: Furthermore, while latency-predicting neurons are, on average, significantly excited by presentations of the DS (Figure 5D and G; t[61]=7.08, p<0.001; 48/62 units excited, 77.4%), latency-predicting neurons in the CS+ task are not (Figure 5E and H; t[13]=2.00, p=0.06650; 7/14 units excited; Bayes factor of 1.27 in favor of the alternative).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test and Bayes factor) and reference to Figures 5E and H.

claims.claim: Latency-predicting neurons are more likely to be excited by the cue in the instrumental task than in the Pavlovian task.
claims.source: Latency-predicting neurons are more likely to be excited by the cue in the instrumental task than in the Pavlovian task (x2 = 4.294, p=0.038246).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison (chi-squared test) of proportions.

claims.claim: The distribution of correlation coefficients was significantly more negative in the instrumental task than in the Pavlovian task.
claims.source: For the population, the distribution of correlation coefficients was significantly more negative in the instrumental task than in the Pavlovian (Figure 5A and C; t[703]=2.0493, p=0.04), though the distribution is more negative in the 300 msec post-cue than in the 300 msec pre-cue in both the instrumental t[313]=–10.81, p<0.001) and Pavlovian tasks (t[390]=–﻿9.52, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison (t-test) and reference to Figures 5A and C.

claims.claim: The distribution of correlation coefficients is more negative in the 300 msec post-cue than in the 300 msec pre-cue in both the instrumental and Pavlovian tasks.
claims.source: For the population, the distribution of correlation coefficients was significantly more negative in the instrumental task than in the Pavlovian (Figure 5A and C; t[703]=2.0493, p=0.04), though the distribution is more negative in the 300 msec post-cue than in the 300 msec pre-cue in both the instrumental t[313]=–10.81, p<0.001) and Pavlovian tasks (t[390]=–﻿9.52, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-tests) for both tasks.

claims.claim: VP firing rates encode some information relating to the subsequent port entry latency in the Pavlovian task, though this encoding is much weaker than in the instrumental task.
claims.source: This suggests that while latency encoding in the Pavlovian task is much weaker, VP firing rates do encode some information relating to the subsequent port entry latency.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the statistical findings showing weak but significant post-cue encoding in the Pavlovian task.

claims.claim: The distribution of correlation coefficients in the Pavlovian task shifted negatively in the 50 msec window prior to cue onset.
claims.source: Surprisingly, we found that the distribution of correlation coefficients in the Pavlovian task shifted negatively in the 50 msec window prior to cue onset (Figure 5F; q=3.532, p<0.05), suggesting that the weak relationship between post-CS+ firing and latency may be accounted for by trial-by-trial variation in firing rates, rather than in phasic cue responses.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 5F.

claims.claim: The weak relationship between post-CS+ firing and latency may be accounted for by trial-by-trial variation in firing rates, rather than in phasic cue responses.
claims.source: Surprisingly, we found that the distribution of correlation coefficients in the Pavlovian task shifted negatively in the 50 msec window prior to cue onset (Figure 5F; q=3.532, p<0.05), suggesting that the weak relationship between post-CS+ firing and latency may be accounted for by trial-by-trial variation in firing rates, rather than in phasic cue responses.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the finding that correlation coefficients shifted before cue onset.

claims.claim: The distribution of correlation coefficients in the DS task did not significantly differ from 0 until the window 50–100 msec post-DS.
claims.source: By contrast, the distribution of correlation coefficients in the DS task did not significantly differ from 0 until the window 50–100 msec post-DS (Figure 5F; q=4.171, p<0.05), when phasic cue excitations are occurring in the bulk of correlated neurons.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 5F.

claims.claim: Encoding of the latency of cue-elicited reward seeking by individual VP units and in the population is much stronger in the instrumental task than in the Pavlovian task.
claims.source: Overall, encoding of the latency of cue-elicited reward seeking by individual VP units and in the population is much stronger in the instrumental task than in the Pavlovian task.
claims.evidence: The claim is a summary inference from multiple statistical comparisons showing stronger latency encoding in the instrumental task.

claims.claim: Variability in post-cue firing did not differ between the instrumental and Pavlovian tasks when comparing the whole population.
claims.source: Variability in post-cue firing did not differ when comparing the whole population (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A; t[704]=–1.16, p=0.24; Bayes factor of 6.10 favoring the null) and was greater in the Pavlovian task when only the cue excited neurons were considered (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B; t[298]=2.75, p=0.0063).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test and Bayes factor) and reference to supplementary figures.

claims.claim: Variability in post-cue firing was greater in the Pavlovian task when only the cue excited neurons were considered.
claims.source: Variability in post-cue firing did not differ when comparing the whole population (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A; t[704]=–1.16, p=0.24; Bayes factor of 6.10 favoring the null) and was greater in the Pavlovian task when only the cue excited neurons were considered (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B; t[298]=2.75, p=0.0063).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) and reference to supplementary figures.

claims.claim: Post-cue port entry latency is more variable in the Pavlovian task.
claims.source: In addition, post-cue port entry latency is more variable in the Pavlovian task (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C and D; z(95354)=−5.82, p<0.001), indicating that weak correlations between post-CS+ firing and latency are not due to low variability in post CS+ port entry latency.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to supplementary figures.

claims.claim: Weak correlations between post-CS+ firing and latency are not due to low variability in post CS+ port entry latency.
claims.source: In addition, post-cue port entry latency is more variable in the Pavlovian task (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C and D; z(95354)=−5.82, p<0.001), indicating that weak correlations between post-CS+ firing and latency are not due to low variability in post CS+ port entry latency.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the finding that latency variability is actually higher in the Pavlovian task.

claims.claim: Instrumentally trained rats moved at greater velocities post-cue than Pavlovian trained rats.
claims.source: Overall, although we found that velocity increased and distance from the port decreased shortly after cue onset for both tasks, instrumentally trained rats moved at greater velocities post-cue (F[1,118]=23.166, p<0.001) and were positioned at further distances from the port at cue onset (F[1,118]=6.99, p=0.009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test) of video tracking data.

claims.claim: Instrumentally trained rats were positioned at further distances from the port at cue onset than Pavlovian trained rats.
claims.source: Overall, although we found that velocity increased and distance from the port decreased shortly after cue onset for both tasks, instrumentally trained rats moved at greater velocities post-cue (F[1,118]=23.166, p<0.001) and were positioned at further distances from the port at cue onset (F[1,118]=6.99, p=0.009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test) of video tracking data.

claims.claim: Rats trained under Pavlovian versus instrumental contingencies did not differ in the likelihood of movement onset during the first 300 ms post cue.
claims.source: Rats trained under Pavlovian versus instrumental contingencies did not differ in the likelihood of movement onset during the first 300 ms post cue in which we assessed neural firing (13.3% of post-DS movement onsets and 8.3% of post-CS+ movement onsets; X2=0.345, p=0.56), and we did not observe a significant difference in movement-onset times (F[1,74]=1.365, p=0.24).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (chi-squared test) of movement onset data.

claims.claim: There was no significant difference in movement-onset times between rats trained under Pavlovian versus instrumental contingencies.
claims.source: Rats trained under Pavlovian versus instrumental contingencies did not differ in the likelihood of movement onset during the first 300 ms post cue in which we assessed neural firing (13.3% of post-DS movement onsets and 8.3% of post-CS+ movement onsets; X2=0.345, p=0.56), and we did not observe a significant difference in movement-onset times (F[1,74]=1.365, p=0.24).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test) of movement onset timing.

claims.claim: Distance encoding significantly predicted latency encoding.
claims.source: We found that the only significant single predictor of latency encoding was distance encoding, in that neurons that had greater post-cue firing rates on trials with shorter port entry latencies, also had greater post-cue firing on trials where the rat was closer to the port at cue onset (Figure 5—figure supplement 5A; F[1,140]=16.295, p<0.001), similar to results previously reported for the nucleus accumbens (McGinty et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test) and reference to supplementary figures.

claims.claim: The relationship between encoding of proximity and vigor depended on training history.
claims.source: This relationship between encoding of proximity and vigor depended on training history (F[1,140]=4.55, p=0.034), as distance encoding in the rats trained under a Pavlovian contingency was not significantly predictive of latency encoding (F[1,44]=2.09, p=0.15), whereas distance encoding robustly predicted latency encoding in instrumentally trained rats (F[1,96]=35.632, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-tests) showing an interaction with training history.

claims.claim: Distance encoding in rats trained under a Pavlovian contingency was not significantly predictive of latency encoding.
claims.source: This relationship between encoding of proximity and vigor depended on training history (F[1,140]=4.55, p=0.034), as distance encoding in the rats trained under a Pavlovian contingency was not significantly predictive of latency encoding (F[1,44]=2.09, p=0.15), whereas distance encoding robustly predicted latency encoding in instrumentally trained rats (F[1,96]=35.632, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test) in the Pavlovian group.

claims.claim: Distance encoding robustly predicted latency encoding in instrumentally trained rats.
claims.source: This relationship between encoding of proximity and vigor depended on training history (F[1,140]=4.55, p=0.034), as distance encoding in the rats trained under a Pavlovian contingency was not significantly predictive of latency encoding (F[1,44]=2.09, p=0.15), whereas distance encoding robustly predicted latency encoding in instrumentally trained rats (F[1,96]=35.632, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test) in the instrumental group.

claims.claim: Latency encoding was not significantly predicted by the degree to which neurons encoded post-cue velocity.
claims.source: Notably, latency encoding was not significantly predicted by the degree to which neurons encoded post-cue velocity (Figure 5—figure supplement 5B; F[1,140]=–0.335, p=0.56) or movement-onset latencies (Figure 5—figure supplement 5C; F[1,140]=1.83, p=0.17).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test) and reference to supplementary figures.

claims.claim: Latency encoding was not significantly predicted by the degree to which neurons encoded movement-onset latencies.
claims.source: Notably, latency encoding was not significantly predicted by the degree to which neurons encoded post-cue velocity (Figure 5—figure supplement 5B; F[1,140]=–0.335, p=0.56) or movement-onset latencies (Figure 5—figure supplement 5C; F[1,140]=1.83, p=0.17).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test) and reference to supplementary figures.

claims.claim: The relationship between distance and latency encoding was modulated by training history, suggesting a greater coupling between these variables and action in the instrumental task.
claims.source: That the relationship between distance and latency encoding was modulated by training history suggests a greater coupling between these variables and action in the instrumental task.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the finding that distance-latency encoding relationship differs by training history.

claims.claim: Rats made port entries at significantly shorter latencies during the reward cue than during the control cue by the end of training.
claims.source: By the end of training, rats made port entries at significantly shorter latencies during the reward cue than during the control cue (main effect of cue: F[1,28]=25.314, p<0.001), regardless of training group (interaction of cue and training: F[1,28]=0.144, p=0.707; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B and F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test) and reference to supplementary figures.

claims.claim: Rats in both training groups increased their probability of port entry preferentially during the reward-related cue versus the control cue.
claims.source: Rats in both training groups increased their probability of port entry preferentially during the reward-related cue versus the control cue (main effect of cue: F[1,28]=951.681, p<0.001), with rats trained under the instrumental contingency reaching a slightly higher response probability during the reward cue once they met training criteria (interaction of cue and training: F[1,28]=5.962, p=0.021; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D and G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test) and reference to supplementary figures.

claims.claim: Rats trained under the instrumental contingency reached a slightly higher response probability during the reward cue once they met training criteria.
claims.source: Rats in both training groups increased their probability of port entry preferentially during the reward-related cue versus the control cue (main effect of cue: F[1,28]=951.681, p<0.001), with rats trained under the instrumental contingency reaching a slightly higher response probability during the reward cue once they met training criteria (interaction of cue and training: F[1,28]=5.962, p=0.021; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D and G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test showing interaction) and reference to supplementary figures.

claims.claim: Rats trained under Pavlovian conditioning required more days to reach training criteria (10.35 ± 0.23) than those trained under an instrumental contingency (9.07 ± 0.24).
claims.source: On average, rats trained under the Pavlovian conditioning required more days to reach training criteria (10.35 ± 0.23) than those trained under an instrumental contingency (9.07 ± 0.24; t[29]=3.839, p<0.001; Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison (t-test) and reference to supplementary figures.

claims.claim: VP inactivation with baclofen and muscimol reduced the probability of port entry during the cue period in the instrumental task.
claims.source: In the instrumental task, inactivation of VP with low doses of the GABA agonists baclofen and muscimol reduced the probability of port entry during the cue period (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2B; main effect of treatment: F[4,130]=28.666, p<0.001; Sidak, p<0.001), and did so more strongly during the DS period than during the NS (interaction between treatment and cue identity: F[4,130]=7.205, p<0.001; DS Sidak, p<0.001; NS Sidak, n.s.).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test and post-hoc tests) and reference to figures.

claims.claim: VP inactivation reduced port entry probability more strongly during the DS period than during the NS in the instrumental task.
claims.source: In the instrumental task, inactivation of VP with low doses of the GABA agonists baclofen and muscimol reduced the probability of port entry during the cue period (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2B; main effect of treatment: F[4,130]=28.666, p<0.001; Sidak, p<0.001), and did so more strongly during the DS period than during the NS (interaction between treatment and cue identity: F[4,130]=7.205, p<0.001; DS Sidak, p<0.001; NS Sidak, n.s.).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing an interaction and selective post-hoc effects.

claims.claim: VP inactivation increased port entry latency during the DS in the instrumental task.
claims.source: VP inactivation also increased port entry latency during the cue (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A; main effect of treatment: F[4,18.254]=4.574, p=0.01) also selectively during the DS (interaction between drug and cue: F[4,23.879]=4.354, p=0.009; DS Sidak, p=0.022; NS Sidak, n.s.).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test and post-hoc tests) and reference to figures.

claims.claim: VP inactivation increased port entry latency selectively during the DS and not the NS in the instrumental task.
claims.source: VP inactivation also increased port entry latency during the cue (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A; main effect of treatment: F[4,18.254]=4.574, p=0.01) also selectively during the DS (interaction between drug and cue: F[4,23.879]=4.354, p=0.009; DS Sidak, p=0.022; NS Sidak, n.s.).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing an interaction and selective post-hoc effects.

claims.claim: VP inactivation during the Pavlovian task reduced the probability of port entry during the cue.
claims.source: Inactivation of VP during the Pavlovian task similarly reduced the probability of port entry during the cue (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 3B; main effect of treatment: F[4,112]=9.904, p<0.001; Sidak p<0.001), and did so selectively during the CS+ period (interaction between treatment and cue identity: F[4,112]=2.622, p=0.039; CS+ Sidak, p<0.001; CS- Sidak, n.s.).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test and post-hoc tests) and reference to figures.

claims.claim: VP inactivation reduced port entry probability selectively during the CS+ period in the Pavlovian task.
claims.source: Inactivation of VP during the Pavlovian task similarly reduced the probability of port entry during the cue (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 3B; main effect of treatment: F[4,112]=9.904, p<0.001; Sidak p<0.001), and did so selectively during the CS+ period (interaction between treatment and cue identity: F[4,112]=2.622, p=0.039; CS+ Sidak, p<0.001; CS- Sidak, n.s.).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing an interaction and selective post-hoc effects.

claims.claim: VP inactivation during the Pavlovian task had no significant effect on port entry latency.
claims.source: In contrast to the instrumental task, VP inactivation during the Pavlovian task had no significant effect on port entry latency (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 3A; main effect of treatment: F[4,21.406]=1.059, p=0.401), regardless of cue identity (interaction between treatment and cue identity: F[4,18.061]=1.742, p=0.185).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test) showing no significant effects and reference to figures.

claims.claim: In both tasks, no drug treatment had any significant effect on port entry behavior during the inter-trial interval.
claims.source: In both tasks, no drug treatment had any significant effect on port entry behavior during the inter-trial interval (main effect of treatment, instrumental task: F[4,65]=2.295, p=0.07; Pavlovian task: F[4,63]=1.526, p=0.205).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-tests) showing no significant effects.

claims.claim: Glutamate receptor antagonism (CNQX-MK801) reduced the probability of port entry during the DS in the instrumental task.
claims.source: Infusions of either a mixture of the glutamate receptor antagonists CNQX and MK801 or the relatively non-selective dopamine receptor antagonist flupenthixol had similar effects to VP inactivation with GABA agonists in both tasks. Glutamate or dopamine blockade reduced the probability of port entry during the cue (Sidak p<0.001 for both), though only the effect of glutamate blockade was selective to the DS (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B; DS Sidak, p<0.001; NS Sidak, p=n .s.) whereas flupenthixol reduced the probability of port entry during both cue types (DS Sidak, p<0.001; NS Sidak, p<0.003).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (post-hoc tests) and reference to figures.

claims.claim: Dopamine receptor antagonism (flupenthixol) reduced the probability of port entry during both the DS and NS in the instrumental task.
claims.source: Infusions of either a mixture of the glutamate receptor antagonists CNQX and MK801 or the relatively non-selective dopamine receptor antagonist flupenthixol had similar effects to VP inactivation with GABA agonists in both tasks. Glutamate or dopamine blockade reduced the probability of port entry during the cue (Sidak p<0.001 for both), though only the effect of glutamate blockade was selective to the DS (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B; DS Sidak, p<0.001; NS Sidak, p=n .s.) whereas flupenthixol reduced the probability of port entry during both cue types (DS Sidak, p<0.001; NS Sidak, p<0.003).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (post-hoc tests) and reference to figures.

claims.claim: Glutamate or dopamine antagonism selectively increased port entry latency during the DS but not during the NS in the instrumental task.
claims.source: Glutamate or dopamine antagonism selectively increased port entry latency during the DS (CNQX-MK801 Sidak, p=0.005; flupenthixol Sidak, p=0.022), but not during the NS.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (post-hoc tests).

claims.claim: Glutamate or dopamine antagonism significantly reduced port entry probability during the CS+ but not during the CS– in the Pavlovian task.
claims.source: In the Pavlovian task, glutamate or dopamine antagonism, like inactivation, significantly reduced port entry probability during the CS+ (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2B; CNQX-MK801 Sidak, p<0.001; flupenthixol Sidak, p=0.043), but not during the CS–, and had no effect on port entry latency (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (post-hoc tests) and reference to figures.

claims.claim: Glutamate or dopamine antagonism had no effect on port entry latency in the Pavlovian task.
claims.source: In the Pavlovian task, glutamate or dopamine antagonism, like inactivation, significantly reduced port entry probability during the CS+ (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2B; CNQX-MK801 Sidak, p<0.001; flupenthixol Sidak, p=0.043), but not during the CS–, and had no effect on port entry latency (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to figures.

claims.claim: Infusions of the NK-1 antagonist WIN51708 had no effect on port entry probability or latency in either task.
claims.source: Infusions of the NK-1 antagonist WIN51708, used to block the effects of substance P, had no effect on port entry probability or latency in either task.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the absence of significant effects in the statistical analysis.

claims.claim: VP neurons do not drive movement invigoration generically, but encode a variable that is manifested by port entry latency after instrumental, but not after Pavlovian training.
claims.source: Our results demonstrate that VP neurons do not drive movement invigoration generically, but encode a variable that is manifested by port entry latency after instrumental, but not after Pavlovian training.
claims.evidence: The claim is a summary inference from the differential encoding and functional effects observed across tasks.

claims.claim: Manipulations of VP alter a wide range of motor behaviors including general locomotion.
claims.source: Manipulations of VP alter a wide range of motor behaviors including general locomotion (Churchill and Kalivas, 1999; Kitamura et al., 2001; Napier and Chrobak, 1992; Root et al., 2015), though reports of locomotor activation linked to VP may be more related to activity in nearby structures such as the rostral preoptic area (Zahm et al., 2014).

results.result: Rats trained in instrumental (DS task) and Pavlovian conditioning tasks showed similar acquisition of cue-elicited reward-seeking behavior, with both groups learning to enter the reward port more frequently and quickly during reward-related cues compared to control cues.
results.evaluation: Claims C13, C76-C79 provide converging evidence from behavioral training data showing that both groups successfully learned their respective tasks with comparable performance levels. Statistical analyses (t-tests, F-tests) support the behavioral equivalence between tasks, though Pavlovian rats required slightly more training days (C79).

results.result: VP neurons respond robustly to reward-related cues in both instrumental and Pavlovian tasks, with 60% of units excited and 27% inhibited by the DS, and 48.7% excited and 20.9% inhibited by the CS+, though the proportion of cue-responsive neurons differed significantly between tasks.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C19 present quantitative electrophysiological data with clear proportions and statistical comparison (chi-squared test, p<0.001). The data demonstrate robust cue responses in both tasks while documenting a significant difference in response proportions, supported by appropriate statistical testing.

results.result: VP neurons encode learned cue value equally in both instrumental and Pavlovian tasks, with both excited and inhibited populations showing significantly greater responses to reward-related cues compared to control cues, and no difference in population auROC distributions between tasks.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C32 provide comprehensive evidence from multiple statistical analyses (t-tests, ROC analyses, Bayes factors) demonstrating that VP neurons encode cue value similarly across tasks. The convergence of individual neuron analyses, population-level statistics, and ROC analyses strongly supports this conclusion.

results.result: DS excited neurons were more likely to be inhibited by the control cue (NS) than CS+ excited neurons were to be inhibited by the CS–, suggesting a more active role for response inhibition in the instrumental task.
results.evaluation: Claim C33 is supported by statistical comparison (chi-squared test, p<0.001) and reference to Figure 3J. The finding suggests task-specific differences in inhibitory encoding, though the functional interpretation remains somewhat speculative.

results.result: VP cue responses predict the likelihood of behavioral responses more strongly in the instrumental task than in the Pavlovian task, with both DS-excited and DS-inhibited populations showing significantly greater firing on trials with responses, while CS+ inhibited neurons did not distinguish between response and no-response trials.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C43 present converging evidence from individual neuron analyses, population statistics (t-tests), and ROC analyses. The data consistently show stronger encoding of response likelihood in the instrumental task, with appropriate statistical support including Bayes factors for null findings (C41).

results.result: VP neurons robustly encode the latency of instrumental reward-seeking responses, with 19.75% of units predicting DS response latency, compared to only 3.57% predicting CS+ response latency. This difference is validated by shuffled control analyses and temporal dynamics showing cue-locked encoding in the instrumental but not Pavlovian task.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C60 provide extensive evidence including correlation analyses, shuffled controls, temporal dynamics, and population-level statistics. The convergence of multiple analytical approaches (individual correlations, shuffled controls, temporal windows, population distributions) strongly supports the task-specific encoding of response latency. The shuffled control analyses (C47-C50) are particularly important for validating the specificity of the findings.

results.result: The weaker correlation between VP firing and response latency in the Pavlovian task is not explained by differences in neural or behavioral variability, as post-cue firing variability was similar or greater in the Pavlovian task, and latency variability was actually higher in the Pavlovian task.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C64 address potential confounds through appropriate statistical analyses (t-tests, Bayes factors). The data rule out variability as an explanation for the task differences, strengthening the interpretation that the differences reflect genuine task-specific encoding rather than measurement artifacts.

results.result: The task-specific encoding of response latency by VP neurons is related to proximity encoding rather than velocity or movement onset, with distance encoding predicting latency encoding only in instrumentally trained rats, suggesting greater coupling between these variables and action in the instrumental task.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C75 present video tracking data and regression analyses showing that proximity encoding, but not velocity or movement onset encoding, predicts latency encoding in a task-dependent manner. The statistical analyses (F-tests, linear mixed models) appropriately test for interactions with training history, supporting the interpretation of task-specific coupling.

results.result: VP inactivation with GABA agonists selectively increases port entry latency during the DS in the instrumental task but has no effect on latency in the Pavlovian task, while reducing port entry probability in both tasks.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C87 present pharmacological manipulation data with appropriate statistical analyses (F-tests, post-hoc comparisons with Sidak corrections). The dissociation between effects on probability (both tasks) and latency (instrumental only) is well-supported and represents a key functional validation of the electrophysiological findings.

results.result: Local disruption of glutamate or dopamine signaling in VP produces effects similar to inactivation, reducing port entry probability and increasing latency in the instrumental task, while only affecting probability in the Pavlovian task.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C92 present pharmacological data showing that glutamate and dopamine receptor antagonism produces task-specific effects similar to inactivation. The statistical support (post-hoc tests with Sidak corrections) is appropriate, and the findings converge with the inactivation results to support a role for these neurotransmitter systems.

results.result: Blocking substance P signaling with NK-1 receptor antagonism has no effect on port entry probability or latency in either task, suggesting that substance P inputs from the nucleus accumbens do not mediate VP contributions to cue-elicited reward seeking.
results.evaluation: Claims C93 and C114 report null findings from pharmacological manipulations. While the absence of effects is clearly stated, the evaluation is limited by the lack of positive controls to verify drug efficacy and receptor occupancy. However, the findings are consistent with the authors' hypothesis about alternative input sources.

results.result: Both glutamate and dopamine signaling in VP play a role in the invigoration of cue-elicited reward seeking, as local disruption of either system reduces the likelihood and speed of reward-seeking responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C116 synthesize the pharmacological findings to conclude that both neurotransmitter systems contribute to VP function. The inference is well-supported by the convergent effects of glutamate and dopamine antagonism on both behavioral measures.

results.result: VP neurons selectively encode and contribute to the vigor of cue-elicited reward-seeking actions when those actions are trained via an instrumental contingency rather than Pavlovian conditioning, indicating that VP encoding is not related to motor invigoration per se but to the ability of cues to invigorate actions upon which reward is contingent.
results.evaluation: Claims C94, C120-C122 represent the main conclusions synthesizing the electrophysiological and pharmacological findings. The conclusions are well-supported by the convergence of neural encoding data (latency prediction, proximity coupling) and functional manipulations (task-specific effects on latency), though the mechanistic interpretation remains somewhat inferential.

results.result: Proximity encoding is similar in both tasks but is only correlated with latency encoding in the instrumental task, and VP activity encodes and contributes to response likelihood in the Pavlovian task, though more weakly than in the instrumental task, potentially through distinct neural mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C103 integrate findings on proximity encoding and response likelihood. C101 is directly supported by statistical analyses, while C102-C103 involve more speculative interpretations about potential mechanisms. The claims are generally supported but include acknowledged uncertainty about underlying mechanisms.

results.result: The ventral pallidum is a critical node in reward circuitry with neurons responding to various reward-related stimuli, and while historically viewed as a motor expression site, recent work suggests a greater role in reward processing, with VP neurons encoding the incentive value of cues.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C12 provide background context from prior literature, all supported by appropriate citations. These claims establish the scientific foundation for the current study and are well-documented in the existing literature.

results.result: VP manipulations alter various motor behaviors, but VP neuron activity may contribute to flexible approach only when it reflects specific decision variables such as incentive value, with the relationship between state and action values potentially differing between instrumental and Pavlovian tasks.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C100 present interpretive discussion of VP function in relation to motor behavior and decision variables. While C95-C96 are supported by citations, C97-C100 are largely speculative interpretations. The claims involve theoretical frameworks that go beyond the direct evidence presented in the study.

results.result: Rostral and caudal VP neurons have different properties and differentially modulate reward-related behaviors, but neurons throughout VP appear to encode cue value and reward seeking similarly across the rostrocaudal axis, though discrete populations may be differentially involved in dissociable behavioral responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C107 discuss anatomical heterogeneity in VP, supported by citations to prior work (C104-C105) and the authors' previous findings (C106). C107 appropriately acknowledges both the similarity in encoding and potential functional heterogeneity, though the latter remains somewhat speculative.

results.result: VP has been conceptualized as an output of the nucleus accumbens, but timing analyses and chemogenetic studies suggest VP cue responses are not simply reflections of accumbens activity, and VP integrates glutamatergic inputs from multiple brain regions with local dopamine modulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C113 and C117-C119 discuss VP circuitry and inputs, all supported by appropriate citations to prior work. The claims establish the anatomical and functional context for understanding VP's role beyond simple relay of accumbens signals.
